Eggs of the Lined forest falcon (Micrastur gilvicollis) incubated at a constant 34 °C [T = 34 °C] require an average of 34 days [ab = 34 days] to hatch, a duration comparable to that of its congener Micrastur ruficollis. This incubation period reflects the typical energetic demands of embryonic development within the genus. Hatchlings emerge with an initial wet body mass of 28 grams [Ww0 = 28 grams], a value also inferred from data on Micrastur ruficollis due to the scarcity of direct measurements for the Lined forest falcon. This modest starting mass underscores the altricial nature of the chicks, which are entirely dependent on parental provisioning during the early nestling phase. The energy required to sustain the developing embryo over the 34-day incubation window is substantial, and the post-hatching growth trajectory quickly accelerates as the young falcons begin to consume prey items delivered by both parents.

Under the active thermal conditions typical of this species' daily activities, estimated at 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the maximum resting metabolic rate of adult Lined forest falcons reaches 189.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 189.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This elevated oxygen consumption supports the high energetic demands of a predatory lifestyle in Neotropical lowland forests. Females ultimately attain an adult wet body mass of 231 grams [Wwi = 231 grams], although field records indicate a broader range of 170 to 262 grams among individuals. This body size is moderate for a forest-falcon, placing the species on the smaller end of the Micrastur spectrum. The metabolic rate measured aligns with predictions for a raptor of this mass, reflecting the costs associated with active hunting and thermoregulation in a warm, humid environment.

Development proceeds rapidly during the nestling stage when ambient conditions are near 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. Fledging occurs 38 days after hatching [tx = 38 days after hatching], a milestone marking the achievement of sustained flight and the beginning of independent movement, though post-fledging parental care often continues for several weeks at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This 38-day period, comparable to that documented in Micrastur ruficollis, allows for substantial feather development and muscle growth before the young leave the nest. The thermal environment at 40 °C likely facilitates rapid growth by reducing the energetic costs of thermoregulation, enabling the chick to allocate more resources toward somatic development. Metabolic rates during this phase are considerably elevated as the fledgling builds the flight musculature necessary for successful prey capture, preparing for the eventual transition to nutritional independence.

Gonadal maturation under the same thermal regime of 40 °C [T = 40 °C] culminates at 114 days after hatching [tp = 114 days after hatching], the age at which young Lined forest falcons become reproductively capable. This 114-day interval represents the period between hatching and the physiological onset of puberty, a duration that allows for the completion of skeletal growth and the development of functional reproductive organs. The first successful breeding event, however, is typically deferred until 694 days since birth [tR = 694 days since birth], a delay that reflects the time required for territory acquisition, pair bonding, and the development of proficient hunting skills necessary to support offspring at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This age at first reproduction, observed at the 40 °C thermal condition, suggests that while sexual maturity is reached relatively early, ecological constraints postpone actual reproductive output.

The species exhibits a maximum recorded lifespan of 4964 days [am = 4964 days] when individuals are maintained at an environmental temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to approximately 13.6 years, places the Lined forest falcon among the longer-lived raptors for its body size. Female reproductive output consists of a single clutch of 3 eggs per nest [N_R_i = 3 eggs per nest] each year, with one nesting attempt annually [F_R_i = one nesting attempt annually]. The combination of a modest clutch size and a single annual breeding event results in a low annual reproductive rate, characteristic of a slow life-history strategy. This reproductive restraint is likely an adaptation to the stochastic availability of prey in the Amazonian understory, where energy investment in each offspring must be high to ensure survival through the extended period of parental dependence.
